title: Energy: work, power and conservation
subject: science
strengths: Most of the class can calculate work done as force times distance.
The class can convert a work and time pair into a power in watts.

modelAnswers.question: A force of 50 N pushes a crate 4 m in the direction of the force. How much work is done?
creditPoints: Scene s1: work = force x distance = 50 x 4 = 200 joules
Carries the working through to the correct final answer

modelAnswers.question: The 200 J of work from question 1 is done in 2 s. Calculate the power.
creditPoints: Scene s2: power = work / time = 200 / 2 = 100 watts
Carries the working through to the correct final answer

commonErrors.misconception: Energy gets used up when work is done.
commonErrors.example: A learner writes that a car that stops has used up all its energy, so the energy no longer exists.

fixIt.prompt: Fix it: name the energy stores before and after the car stops, and state what happened to the total.
fixIt.corrected: The chemical energy became kinetic energy and then heat in the brakes and surroundings; the total energy is unchanged - it changed form, it was not destroyed.

commonErrors.misconception: Energy gets used up when work is done.
commonErrors.example: On the exit ticket, a learner says the falling mass loses its energy as it falls because the GPE decreases.

fixIt.prompt: Fix it: track the 98 J of GPE as the mass falls and state the KE just before landing.
fixIt.corrected: The 98 J of GPE becomes 98 J of KE as the mass falls; just before landing the KE is 98 J and the total energy is still 98 J.

nextSteps: Reteach conservation of energy with a before-and-after energy tally for every question.
Practise stating the energy change in words before substituting numbers.
